With 15,000 merchants using order numbers such as sequential invoice IDs as keys, collisions on a merchant-agnostic Redis key are likely in normal use. Each one returns another merchant's response and suppresses a payment, and a reused key with a changed body gets the stale response instead of HTTP 422.

recommendation.change_summary: In 9.2, change the Redis key to idem:resp:{merchant_id}:{idempotency_key} (or a hash of the pair). Store the request_hash alongside the cached response and compare it on every hit, returning 422 on a mismatch. Update the Section 24 idempotency decision text to match.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Restores FR-5 and P3 on every path, prevents cross-merchant disclosure (NFR-7) and prevents lost payments.
recommendation.issue: The fast-path cache key leaves out merchant identity and the response is returned without checking the request hash.
recommendation.rationale: P3 and FR-5 require deduplication on (merchant, key) and a 422 for a reused key with a different body. The fast path as written breaks both and leaks data between merchants.
recommendation.verification: Extend the FR-5 test with (a) two merchants sending the same key with different bodies, each getting their own payment, and (b) the same merchant resending a completed key with a modified body while Redis is warm, which must return 422.

findings.statement: Section 9.2 writes the final response to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} and returns it on any hit without consulting DynamoDB, so neither the merchant identity (P3) nor the request hash (FR-5's 422 rule) is checked on the fast path. Section 9.1 explicitly accepts merchant order and invoice numbers as keys. If two merchants use the same key, the second merchant receives the first merchant's payment object (cross-merchant disclosure of amounts, BIN and last 4) and its own payment is silently never created. The FR-5 acceptance test uses one merchant and an identical body, so it would not catch this.
findings.title: Redis idempotency fast path is keyed without merchant and skips the body-hash check

(b) Move the FRV-1 call that needs PAN into a CDE-resident relay with its own service identity, add it and FRV-1 (as a third-party service provider) to 12.2, and make PCI responsibilities part of the Backlog 4 contract. It also explains why Section 5 exposes detokenise across the segmentation boundary to the core VPC. As written, the Fraud Hook, the Orchestrator path that calls it, and the core VPC fall into CDE scope, so NFR-5 cannot be assessed against Section 12.2. Sharing a service role also breaks P9. PAN goes to a third party whose data processing agreement is still pending (Backlog 4).

A timeout or 5xx is an ambiguous outcome. If the first acquirer approved, cascading produces a second approval while the first hold stays live and unrecorded, which ties up cardholder funds and leaves an attempt that cannot be reconciled.

recommendation.change_summary: In 11.1, split Retryable into 'definite' (connection refused, explicit soft decline) and 'ambiguous' (timeout, 5xx). Before cascading an ambiguous attempt, the adapter sends an authorization reversal or a status inquiry for it. In 11.2, replace 'logged and discarded' with: a late approval on a superseded attempt triggers an automatic reversal and an audit event, and is tracked until confirmed. Correct the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' sentence.
recommendation.expected_benefit: No double holds on cardholder funds, and every acquirer-side authorization is accounted for (FR-2, FR-10, P1).
recommendation.issue: Ambiguous outcomes (timeout, 5xx) are cascaded as if they were definite failures, and late approvals are dropped.
recommendation.rationale: FR-2 and P1 require the payment record to be the single truth. An authorization at the acquirer that the platform does not know about breaks this and harms cardholders.
recommendation.verification: Add an FR-7 case in which the simulator approves attempt 1 at 2,600 ms. Pass if a reversal is sent for attempt 1 and exactly one authorization stays live at the simulator.

findings.statement: Sections 11.1 and 11.2 cascade immediately on a 2,500 ms timeout or an HTTP 5xx, and discard any response that arrives after the timeout. In both cases the first acquirer may already have approved. A second approval then puts two holds on the cardholder's funds, and the first is never reversed because the ledger and state machine know only the approved attempt. The claim that cascading 'cannot create a duplicate charge' holds only for definite failures such as connection refused. The sweeper in 20.3 handles payments stuck in AUTHORISING, not orphaned approvals on attempts that were superseded.
findings.title: Cascading after a timeout or 5xx can leave duplicate live authorizations; late approvals are discarded

At the design peak, 55% of 2,000 TPS is about 1,100 card TPS, and each payment needs several HSM operations (tokenise wrap, HMAC fingerprint, CVC wrap, one unwrap per attempt). One HSM therefore carries several thousand operations per second with no redundancy, and the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM is never reached at the 2027 target.

next_step.action: Prototype a two-HSM cluster and run the operations-per-second benchmark and the cross-region backup-restore drill before Phase 2 exits.

recommendation.change_summary: In 12.3, provision at least two HSMs in different AZs from launch, and update the Section 24 decision. Classify Vault 503 as a non-cascading platform error with fast failure, rather than retryable. Add to 20.2 a standby CDE in ap-southeast-3: a CloudHSM cluster restored from a cross-region backup copy, replicated Vault storage, and Card Adapter steps in the failover runbook. Benchmark HSM operations per second for the 2,000 TPS card mix.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Card acceptance survives the loss of one AZ (NFR-3) and the loss of the region (NFR-4), and HSM capacity is confirmed for NFR-1.
recommendation.issue: Card acceptance depends on one HSM in one AZ, has no cross-region path, and a Vault outage triggers cascades that add load.
recommendation.rationale: NFR-3 allows about 22 minutes of downtime a month. An AZ or HSM loss with backup-based recovery, or a regional failover without a CDE, exceeds that and NFR-4's 30-minute RTO.
recommendation.verification: A chaos test that terminates the AZ-a HSM during NFR-1 load must keep card success within the SLO. The NFR-4 game day must include card authorizations in ap-southeast-3. The HSM benchmark must show at least 2× headroom at the peak operation rate.

findings.statement: The KEKs sit on one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. Section 12.1 does not cache DEKs, so every tokenise and detokenise needs the HSM: losing that HSM or that AZ stops all card acceptance (about 55% of attempts) until a new HSM is built from the daily backup. This undercuts the three-AZ posture in 20.1 and NFR-3. Section 12.3 maps the Vault's 503 to a retryable outcome, so each payment cascades up to three times against the same failed Vault, multiplying load when the HSM is degraded. Section 20.2 does not cover the CDE, Vault data or HSM in ap-southeast-3, so a regional failover cannot restore card payments within the NFR-4 target of 30 minutes. This challenges the confirmed decision 'one HSM at launch'.
findings.title: Single CloudHSM in one AZ is a single point of failure for all card payments, and the Vault has no DR region

recommendation.change_summary: The accountable owner chooses either (a) restating NFR-4 as a bounded RPO (for example ≤ 1 s for the database) plus mandatory post-failover recovery of in-flight authorizations from acquirer reports and reversal or recording of orphans, or (b) a synchronous cross-region commit design and its latency cost. Separately, add idempotency_key and request_hash columns to payment, with a unique constraint on (merchant_account_id, idempotency_key), so the 20.2 rebuild is possible. Document regional failover as excluded from, or in conflict with, NFR-3.
recommendation.expected_benefit: An honest, testable DR objective (NFR-4), FR-5 that holds across failover, and an NFR-3 budget consistent with the DR plan.
recommendation.issue: NFR-4 is unachievable with the chosen replication, and the idempotency rebuild depends on data that is not stored.
recommendation.rationale: Leaving an unachievable RPO in place means the NFR-4 game day passes only if replication lag happens to be near zero, while real failovers can lose authorizations and produce duplicate charges.
recommendation.verification: Run the NFR-4 game day under NFR-1 load and compare acquirer-simulator authorizations with the promoted ledger. Replay merchant retries with the same keys after failover and check that no second authorization is made.

findings.statement: NFR-4 requires an RPO of zero for authorizations and ledger postings on loss of a region, but 20.2 relies on asynchronous Aurora Global Database replication with lag under one second. Authorizations acknowledged in that last second exist at the acquirer but not in the promoted database. Section 20.2 also says idempotency state is 'reconstructed from the payment table', but the payment table in Section 19 stores no idempotency key or request hash. After failover, merchant retries therefore create new payments and new authorizations, breaking FR-5. In addition, one 30-minute failover uses more than NFR-3's monthly downtime budget of about 22 minutes.
findings.title: Zero RPO on region loss cannot hold with async replication, and idempotency state cannot be rebuilt

recommendation.change_summary: Check the per-partition throughput limit, write-unit metering and LSI item-collection limits against AWS documentation. The likely change in 9.2/9.3 is a partition key of merchant_id#idempotency_key with no LSI: serve the back-office 'recent requests' view from a GSI or the event bus, and keep large response bodies out of the hot item. Correct the 9.3 arithmetic.
recommendation.expected_benefit: Confirms that NFR-1 is achievable for the largest merchant, or forces the key design to change before Phase 3.
recommendation.issue: The capacity argument for the hottest partition key rests on an unverified limit and leaves out item size and the LSI's size constraints.

findings.statement: Section 9.3 assumes one partition sustains 10,000 WCU per second and that M-0001 needs about 1,800 WCU (two writes per request). The completion write, however, stores a response body of up to 4 KB, so if writes are metered by item size it costs several units. The per-partition figure also needs checking against AWS's published limits, which the reviewer expects to be much lower. Keying by merchant_id with an LSI also limits how far one partition-key value can grow or split. M-0001 writes about 4.7 M items a day, which is roughly 20 GB held under the 24-hour TTL. If any of these limits bind, conditional puts for 45% of peak traffic are throttled at campaign peaks, breaking NFR-1.
findings.title: DynamoDB idempotency table: per-partition capacity and LSI sizing for the largest merchant are unverified

findings.statement: Section 12.4 and NFR-6 state that PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept in encrypted form until settlement. On that basis the design keeps CVC for up to 72 hours for cascades and later incremental authorizations. The reviewer understands the standard's allowance to be tied to completing authorization, not settlement, but this needs QSA confirmation. If the reviewer is right, the Vault stores prohibited data and NFR-5 fails, and NFR-6 and its test would themselves enforce the non-compliant rule.
findings.title: Keeping CVC encrypted until settlement (up to 72 h) relies on an unverified reading of PCI DSS

recommendation.expected_benefit: Prevents payout diversion and enforces P9 in the merchant plane.
recommendation.issue: The highest-value fraud path, changing where payouts go, has weaker controls than the internal console.
recommendation.rationale: P9 requires money-moving permissions to be separated, and FR-17 payouts go to the 'registered' account. Without verification and multi-party control, a takeover means direct financial loss.
recommendation.verification: Extend the FR-13 role-matrix test: a change without step-up fails, a Finance change stays pending until an Owner approves, and the FR-17 test shows no payout to an unverified account.

findings.statement: Section 18.4 lets one Finance or Owner user change the payout bank account in the portal. The only notice goes to the person who made the change, and there is no step-up authentication, second approver, cooling-off period or verification gate, even though the payout account entity has a verified_at field. MFA is enforced only for Owners, so a phished Finance password is enough to redirect a merchant's next payout. The Finance role also both issues refunds and edits the payout account, against P9's separation of money-moving duties. The back-office console (18.5) already requires a second approver for comparable actions; the merchant plane does not.
findings.title: Payout bank-account change by a single user, MFA optional, notification only to the changer

Option (b): introduce an overall authorization deadline, with a per-attempt timeout well under 2,500 ms and a cascade only when the remaining budget covers the next acquirer's p95. recommendation.issue: NFR-2 and the cascade policy cannot both hold with the current timeout and baseline retry rate.
recommendation.rationale: Either the requirement or the cascade mechanism has to change, and that is a product trade-off between authorization uplift and latency.
recommendation.verification: Run the NFR-2 benchmark with 3.8% retryable injection and a realistic timeout share, and report p99 separately for cascaded and non-cascaded payments.

findings.statement: Section 21.1 leaves cascading out of the p99 budget on the grounds that fewer than 1% of card payments cascade. Section 10.5, however, reports 3.8% retryable outcomes, and each of these cascades. The cascade path is therefore inside the slowest 1%, which also includes timeouts. An attempt that times out waits 2,500 ms before the next one, already more than the 1,500 ms limit in NFR-2, which explicitly includes cascades. The NFR-2 acceptance test injects 3.8% retryable outcomes, so the design as written should fail its own test.
findings.title: The latency budget leaves out cascades, but 3.8% retryable outcomes put the cascade path inside p99

findings.statement: The matcher starts only after every expected file has arrived. ACQ-TH1 delivers at 06:30 ICT (07:30 SGT), and at 2025 volume matching takes 45 minutes and reports 15 more, so reports are ready around 08:30 SGT even before volume roughly doubles by 2027. NFR-8 is therefore missed every day. Because matching gates SETTLED transitions and payouts, a single late or missing provider file holds up reconciliation and FR-17 payouts for all markets. At 99.9% auto-match, several thousand exceptions a day go to Finance Operations, and no capacity or service level is defined for handling them.
findings.title: All-files-received batch matching misses the NFR-8 08:00 SGT deadline, and one late file blocks every payout

findings.statement: If FRV-1 times out or returns an error, payments for LOW and MEDIUM risk-tier merchants are accepted unscored. With a 150 ms hard timeout and the vendor SLA not yet agreed (Backlog 4), a vendor brownout during a campaign peak would let most card volume through without scoring. P8 treats fraud signals as optional enrichment, while FR-9 requires every card payment to be scored, and the design names no risk owner, exposure cap or alert for the unscored share.
findings.title: Fraud fallback accepts LOW and MEDIUM merchant payments unscored, with no limit or risk owner

findings.statement: Section 9.2 relies on the stuck-payment sweeper to recover IN_PROGRESS records, but Section 20.3 sweeps only payments in AUTHORISING. A pod that crashes after the conditional put but before the payment is created, or while the payment is in CREATED or REQUIRES_ACTION, leaves a lock with no payment_id that nothing resolves. The merchant then receives 409 for that key for up to 24 hours, which breaks FR-5's promise of the identical response and blocks the payment.

findings.statement: Personal data from customers in five markets is stored only in ap-southeast-1 and replicated to ap-southeast-3. FRV-1 receives IP address, device fingerprint and hashed email and phone (pseudonymous personal data) while its DPA is still pending. Audit records with before and after values are kept immutable for five years. The design records no transfer basis per market, no field-level retention mapping, and no way to reconcile immutable audit payloads with the retention limits NFR-7 requires. Its only check is a DPO sign-off in Phase 9, after the data flows are built. Whether any market law restricts these transfers is unverified here.
findings.title: No cross-border transfer or retention analysis for personal data sent to Singapore, Jakarta DR and FRV-1

findings.no_change_rationale: The design meets FR-10 and P5 through database-enforced mechanisms rather than convention, and keeps the payment path available when the event bus fails, so no change is justified.
findings.statement: Each state transition, its ledger journal and its outbox row are committed in one PostgreSQL transaction. UPDATE and DELETE are revoked on journal and posting, and a nightly recomputation is checked against the asynchronous balance projection, with payouts frozen on any mismatch. This removes dual-write failure modes, survives MSK outages (20.4), and avoids hot-row contention at 2,000 TPS. It directly serves FR-10, P1, P5 and P7.
findings.title: Atomic state, ledger and outbox commit with an append-only ledger enforced in the database
